newsitem.title: UK: Dlr/yen bounces back above 113 yen after stumble.
newsitem.headline: Dlr/yen bounces back above 113 yen after stumble.

text.p: The dollar bounced near two-yen from five-month troughs hit in early Europe and stood above 113 yen at midday after Japanese officials warned the yen's rise had been too rapid and a rate rise is not likely in the short-term.
"The dollar has recovered after Sakakibara (Eisuke) said the yen's rise had been too rapid," said Alessandra Stagliano, economist at Daiwa Europe.

Sakakibara, director-general of the Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, and know as "Mr Yen" for his power over markets, said the pace of the yen's strengthening against the dollar was too rapid and that volatility was undesirable.
Sakakibara, speaking to Reuters, said too much volatility in foreign exchange markets was undesirable and that Japan would "deal appropriately" with such excessive volatility.
At 1030 GMT dollar/yen was trading at 113.56/3.66, down 2.30 yen from 115.93 in late Europe on Monday, but up from session lows of 111.98, the dollar's lowest level since December 1996.

Dollar/yen skidded earlier on reports Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Partly (LDP) committee was mulling the possibility of requesting higher discount rates from the Bank of Japan in order to rationalise government-affiliated financial institutions.
Dollar/mark was steady at 1.6981/85, but off early lows.

"It is true that the committee is talking about requesting a rise in the official discount rate, but we are still in the process of wrapping it up and have not decided whether to include it in the proposals or not," an LDP official said.
Later on Tuesday, however, Japan's Jiji news agency quoted an LDP official as saying that now is not the time for the BoJ to tighten its credit policy.

Taku Yamasaki, chairman of the Liberal Democratic Party's policy research council, was also quoted by Jiji as saying that it was inappropriate to discuss the possibility of a rise in Japan's official discount rate now.
But even with rates at record lows, Japan's official discount rate has been at a low of 0.5 percent since September 1995, and analysts said a rise in the short-term is unlikely.
"A rise in rates in the short-term is unlikely. If anything, the rapid strengthening of the yen is negative for the economy and it points to no hike in rates," said Daiwa's Stagliano.
"This is - in effect - a tightening," she added.

The U.S. currency has taken a battering this month, collapsing from 4 1/2 year highs around 127.46 yen. Some analysts say the slide in dollar/yen reflects a revaluation of the yen rather than a weakening of the dollar, with more to come.
